questions.q: What is the most accurate description of a qubit's state?
options: A vector in a 2-dimensional complex vector space, written a|0⟩+b|1⟩, where a and b are complex amplitudes
A single bit that is secretly 0 or 1 but temporarily unknown to the observer
Two independent classical bits running in parallel
A probability value between 0 and 1 representing how 'quantum' the bit currently is
questions.explain: A qubit's state is a vector in a 2D complex vector space, a|0⟩+b|1⟩, not a hidden classical value and not a single probability number. The amplitudes a and b are complex, which is what later allows interference.

questions.q: Why must the coefficients a and b in |ψ⟩=a|0⟩+b|1⟩ be complex numbers rather than plain non-negative probabilities?
options: Because quantum computers can only store complex numbers in their hardware, never real ones
There is no real reason -- real, non-negative probabilities would work exactly as well
Because complex numbers are easier to normalize than real numbers
Because complex numbers carry a phase, and phase is what allows amplitudes to interfere (reinforce or cancel) -- something plain probabilities cannot do
questions.explain: The complex phase carried by amplitudes is what allows constructive and destructive interference between computational paths -- the core mechanism every quantum algorithm exploits. Plain probabilities can never cancel each other out the way amplitudes can.

questions.q: For the state |ψ⟩=0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩, is this a valid quantum state, and why?
options: Yes, because 0.6 and 0.8 are both positive numbers less than 1
No, because a valid state requires both amplitudes to be equal
No, because 0.6 and 0.8 don't add up to 1
Yes, because 0.6²+0.8² = 0.36+0.64 = 1, satisfying the normalization condition
questions.explain: Validity requires |a|²+|b|²=1, not a+b=1. Here 0.6²+0.8²=0.36+0.64=1 exactly, so this is a valid normalized state (verified by direct computation).

questions.q: If the amplitude on |0⟩ in a valid single-qubit state is changed from 0.6 to 0.6 while the amplitude on |1⟩ is changed from 0.8 to 0.9, what happens?
options: The state remains valid, since both numbers are still less than 1
The state becomes a classical bit instead of a qubit
Nothing changes, because amplitudes are not required to satisfy any constraint
The state becomes invalid, since 0.6²+0.9² = 0.36+0.81 = 1.17, which does not equal 1
questions.explain: 0.6²+0.9²=0.36+0.81=1.17, which is not 1, so normalization fails and this pair of amplitudes does not describe a physically valid qubit state.

questions.q: How does the state space of n qubits compare to the state space of n classical bits?
options: The size of a qubit register's state space has nothing to do with the number of qubits
n qubits span a 2ⁿ-dimensional complex vector space, while n classical bits can only ever be in exactly one of 2ⁿ discrete states at a time
n qubits can only represent n possible states, fewer than classical bits
n qubits and n classical bits have exactly the same state space, just with different notation
questions.explain: n qubits together live in a 2ⁿ-dimensional complex vector space (subject to one normalization constraint), a structurally richer object than an n-bit classical register, which is always in exactly one of 2ⁿ fixed values.
